To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) term discrimination values calculated using the cosine coefficient of similarity are highly correlated with the term frequencies of the terms; (2) term discrimination values using other similarity coefficients are less well correlated with term frequencies; (3) term discrimination values can be used as a means to weight terms in the retrieval formula; and (4) the cosine coefficient is the most effective similarity coefficient to use in term discrimination calculations.

term discrimination values are not a good basis for term selection, that term discrimination values can be used to rank terms in a manner that improves retrieval effectiveness, that term discrimination is not a good basis on which to select or rank terms in a Boolean retrieval system, and that the use of exact term discrimination in the calculation of the weights of terms in a document is a feasible alternative to the use of the term frequency of a term in a document.

the relationship between the term frequency of a term and its discrimination value depends on the similarity measure used, and that the discrimination of a term can be calculated exactly and rapidly using a new algorithm.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the development of a new algorithm for the calculation and use of term discrimination values.
the development of an effective method for the automatic selection and weighting of terms for use in document retrieval systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
term discrimination values should be computed using the exact formula and a measure of inter-document similarity that takes into account the number of documents in which a particular term occurs.

the use of the cosine coefficient for the calculation of discrimination values is to be preferred to the use of the Jaccard coefficient, and that this conclusion is valid for a wide variety of retrieval systems.

, for the type of document collection studied, term discrimination values calculated from a cosine interdocument similarity measure, and based on the exact number of documents in which each term occurs, are a good measure of the relative importance of index terms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
term discrimination is not a useful index term weighting method, and should not be used.

the use of term frequency as the sole criterion for the weighting of index terms is a reasonable approximation for the case of the cosine similarity measure, but that it is not a satisfactory approximation for the case where the similarity measure is based on the Euclidean or Manhattan distance measures.

term frequency is an important term weighting parameter, but that the use of discrimination values as a weighting factor in automatic document retrieval is limited by the fact that discrimination values are strongly dependent upon the type and parameters of the inter-document similarity measure.
The main takeaway from our work is that

term discrimination values are not necessarily a good measure of the importance of an indexing term, as the relationship between discrimination and term frequency depends on the similarity measure used for the calculation.
term discrimination values can be calculated in an exact fashion and that they are a useful tool in the design of automatic retrieval systems.
the choice of similarity measure should be based on the type of discrimination values that are to be used.
